newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BAA expects 102 mln stg windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BAA expects 102 mln stg windfall tax.

text.p: Airports operator BAA Plc said on Tuesday it expects to get a bill for 102 million pounds under the new British government's windfall tax on profits made by former state-owned utilities.
Previously the company had estimated its liability at between 70 and 100 million pounds after the new Labour government announced the proposed formula for assessing the one-off tax on July 2.
BAA said it was charging 102 million pounds as a provision for the tax on its first-quarter net profits, which were up 7.1 percent at 105 million pounds.
But the actual bill, which will be payable in two instalments, at the end of 1997 and 1998, was still subject to final agreement with the Inland Revenue.
"That is the worst-case scenario," finance director Russell Walls told Reuters. "Some companies are providing for the tax and some are not. We just took the view 'let's get it out of the way.'"
BAA's share price was up 17-1/2p on the news at 578p by 0850 GMT with analysts saying they welcomed the speedy write-off while underlying results were in line with expectations.
Pre-tax profits for the three months to June 30 rose 4.5 percent to 136 million pounds ($221.7 million) on turnover up 5.7 percent at 367 million pounds.
The company said first-quarter, pre-tax profits would have been up by 13.1 percent but growth was held back by several factors.

A new five-year price cap on regulated airline charges at its London airports took effect in April. There were changes in accounting for interest charges on preliminary costs for a proposed fifth terminal at London Heathrow and BAA said the phasing out of differentials in peak and off-peak traffic charges depressed profit comparisons by eight million pounds.
"The results were pretty much as expected," said Nigel Davies, analyst at brokers Panmure Gordon.
"But if you adjust the figures for the rebalance of the landing charges then operating profit would have been up 10.8 percent and traffic growth of 7.8 percent was significant," he said.

"The shares look cheap at these levels. They are only on a six percent premium to the (overall) market where historically they have traded up to a 35 percent premium and we certainly prefer them to British Airways."

Walls said that the overall financial effects of the new regulatory regime was likely to depress operating profits by about 15 million pounds in the current year compared to last year's operating result of 491 million pounds.

But operating profits in the first quarter rose 5.7 percent, to 147 million pounds, boosted by a 7.8 percent rise in passenger traffic at its seven British airports over the period, to 26.5 million passengers.
Income from regulated charges increased by 4.2 percent to 136 million pounds while net revenue from its extensive airport retailing operations grew by eight percent to 113 million pounds.
The strength of sterling encouraged more people to travel abroad but deterred more spending in airport shops, reflected by the slowdown in growth in the spend-per-passenger in the quarter.
"We would say there is a net increase to the number of people who travel when the pound is strong but there is a tendency, particularly for foreign travellers, to buy less," Walls said.
Nevertheless he said traffic growth remained strong in July, despite the three-day cabin crew strike at British Airways Plc, since many BA passengers were transferred to other carriers.
"The passenger numbers are very strong...and we expect that to continue," said Walls.
